meta.description: Paintings influenced by, or critically connected to, Claude Monet's Water Lilies (Les Nymphéas). Intended as edge targets for a d3/React visualization whose source catalog is water_lilies_catalog.json. Monet painting IDs use the Wildenstein catalogue raisonné numbers (e.g. W.1973) present in water_lilies_catalog.json's `catalog_number` field; Orangerie panels use the 'First room: N' / 'Second room: N' keys from the same file.

image_url_status_legend.resolved: A real, stable image URL is present in image_url.
image_url_status_legend.placeholder_copyright_estate: Image rights held by artist estate or foundation; no licensed public endpoint. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
image_url_status_legend.placeholder_no_api: Institution holds the work but does not publish an open image API or IIIF endpoint. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.

image_rights_legend.public_domain: Work is out of copyright; reproduction rights generally free.
image_rights_legend.copyright_estate: Under artist-estate copyright; requires license for non-editorial use.
image_rights_legend.fair_use_educational: Reproduced under U.S. fair-use / educational exemption at small size.

connection_type_legend.all-over: Compositional evenness, no figure/ground hierarchy (Greenberg's Monet→Pollock argument).
connection_type_legend.horizonless: No anchoring horizon line; the pond-surface trick abstracted.
connection_type_legend.scale-immersive: Room-filling canvases that envelop the viewer (Grandes Décorations → Rothko Chapel, Newman).
connection_type_legend.color-field: Large expanses of modulated color doing the expressive work.
connection_type_legend.direct-homage: Artist explicitly quotes the Water Lilies motif.
connection_type_legend.biographical: Artist lived near Giverny / visited the pond / knew Monet's circle.
connection_type_legend.loose-critical: Typological or retrospective critical link only.

connection_strength_legend.direct: Artist said it (letters, interviews, studio statements).
connection_strength_legend.documented: Scholar or curator has proved it with archival evidence, or a major museum has staged the comparison in a curated exhibition.
connection_strength_legend.critical: Critic or curator drew the link at the time or since, without an explicit artist statement.

paintings.title: Autumn Rhythm (Number 30)
paintings.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
paintings.connection_claim: Critic Clement Greenberg's 1957 essay 'The Later Monet' argued that Pollock's even, edge-to-edge drips continued the visual logic of Monet's late Water Lilies, where no horizon line anchors the picture and no single point of focus organizes it. The 2018 Musée de l'Orangerie exhibition 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet' staged this lineage with Pollock's drip paintings hung in dialogue with Monet's late canvases.
paintings.citation: Clement Greenberg, 'The Later Monet,' Art News Annual 26 (1957), 132–148; Hearne Pardee, 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet,' The Brooklyn Rail (October 2018).

paintings.title: One: Number 31, 1950
paintings.medium: oil and enamel on unprimed canvas
paintings.collection: Museum of Modern Art, New York
paintings.connection_claim: MoMA director Alfred Barr acquired Monet's Water Lilies in 1955 and called it a bridge between early Impressionism and the abstract art being made in New York, hanging it near Pollock's One: Number 31 to make the lineage visible. Critics from Greenberg onward read Pollock's veil of dripped paint as a continuation of Monet's atmospheric late surfaces, and Apollo Magazine's 2018 review of the Orangerie show identified this Barr–Pollock pairing as the curatorial premise that launched the whole Monet-as-Abstract-Expressionist-precursor argument.
paintings.citation: Matthew Holman, 'How Monet's water lilies took root across the pond,' Apollo Magazine, July 17, 2018; Alfred H. Barr Jr., MoMA acquisition file for Water Lilies, 1955.

paintings.title: The Deep
paintings.collection: Centre Pompidou, Paris
paintings.connection_claim: The Deep was loaned by the Centre Pompidou to the 2018 Orangerie show as a contested case. Critic David Anfam argued in The Art Newspaper that the central white tear opening into a black ground reads more as Clyfford Still than as Monet, while Apollo's Sebastian Smee instead saw the same 'enigmatic abyss' as the dark water of Monet's late Japanese Footbridge canvases.
paintings.citation: David Anfam, 'What debt does mid-century American abstract painting owe to Monet?,' The Art Newspaper, August 17, 2018.

paintings.title: No. 14, 1960
paintings.collection: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA)
paintings.connection_claim: Curator William Seitz, in MoMA's 1960 catalogue 'Monet: Seasons and Moments,' was among the first to read Rothko's wall-sized color rectangles as the post-war American counterpart to the Orangerie's enveloping panels: viewers stand inside color rather than in front of an image. In No. 14, the orange and blue blocks dissolve at their edges into the surrounding ground, refusing the figure-and-ground separation of traditional easel painting in the way Seitz argued Monet had pioneered.
paintings.citation: William C. Seitz, Monet: Seasons and Moments, exh. cat. (New York: The Museum of Modern Art, 1960); Hearne Pardee, 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet,' The Brooklyn Rail (October 2018).

paintings.title: Rothko Chapel, North Apse Triptych
paintings.medium: oil and mixed media on canvas
paintings.dimensions: central panel 457.2 × 304.8 cm; flanking panels each c. 335.3 × 243.8 cm
paintings.collection: Rothko Chapel, Houston, Texas
paintings.connection_claim: Critics including Robert Rosenblum read the Rothko Chapel as a non-religious American descendant of the Orangerie's two oval rooms: a purpose-built environment where the viewer stands inside a continuous painted field rather than facing discrete pictures. The Chapel's dim, calibrated light, like Monet's diffused skylight at the Orangerie, is engineered so the panels reveal themselves slowly to adjusted eyes.
paintings.citation: Robert Rosenblum, Modern Painting and the Northern Romantic Tradition: Friedrich to Rothko (Harper & Row, 1975), chapter 7.

paintings.title: No. 61 (Rust and Blue)
paintings.collection: Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles
paintings.connection_claim: Greenberg's 1955 essay 'American-Type Painting' framed Rothko, Newman and Still as the first American painters to break with Cubism by following Monet's all-over color sensation rather than Cubist construction. In No. 61, the rust and blue rectangles float on a thinly washed ground that bleeds into them at the edges, denying spatial depth in the way Greenberg argued Monet had bequeathed to the New York School.
paintings.citation: Clement Greenberg, '"American-Type" Painting,' Partisan Review 22:2 (1955), 179–196; reprinted in Art and Culture (Beacon Press, 1961).
paintings._note: Rothko Chapel (1971) carries the Orangerie oval-room immersive logic further; see rothko-chapel-north-triptych-1966.

paintings.title: Vir Heroicus Sublimis
paintings.collection: Museum of Modern Art, New York
paintings.connection_claim: After his 1954 Paris visit to the Orangerie, Greenberg argued that Newman pursued the same enveloping, peripheral-vision experience Monet engineered there. Newman's 1951 wall statement at Betty Parsons Gallery directed viewers to stand close to his large paintings, a curatorial counterpart to Monet's panels that Greenberg saw as evidence of the same impulse, even though Newman never named Monet himself.
paintings.citation: Clement Greenberg, '"American-Type" Painting,' Partisan Review 22:2 (1955); Barnett Newman, wall statement for his second exhibition at Betty Parsons Gallery, April 1951; reprinted in John P. O'Neill (ed.), Barnett Newman: Selected Writings and Interviews (Knopf, 1990), 178.

paintings.title: La Grande Vallée XIV (For a Little While)
paintings.collection: Centre Pompidou, Paris
paintings.image_url_comment: Centre Pompidou publishes no open IIIF image endpoint. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Mitchell lived from 1968 until her death at Vétheuil, in a house overlooking Monet's earlier property, and the 2022 Fondation Louis Vuitton exhibition 'Monet–Mitchell' paired her late multi-panel paintings directly with the Orangerie panels. Mitchell herself rejected the comparison, telling Deborah Solomon 'I bought this house because I liked the view, not out of any love for Monet,' but the curators presented her late polyptychs as the closest twentieth-century parallel to Monet's installation.
paintings.citation: Suzanne Pagé, Marianne Mathieu, Angeline Scherf et al. (eds.), Monet–Mitchell, exh. cat. (Paris: Fondation Louis Vuitton / Hazan, 2022).

paintings.title: Mountains and Sea
paintings.medium: oil and charcoal on unprimed canvas
paintings.collection: Helen Frankenthaler Foundation, on extended loan to the National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C.
paintings.connection_claim: Frankenthaler's soak-stain technique, in which thinned pigment soaks directly into the raw canvas weave, was read by Greenberg and Michael Fried as the American counterpart to Monet's late ponds, where water, reflection, and painted surface collapse into a single optical layer. The 2018 Orangerie exhibition included two large Frankenthalers from 1963 (Riverhead and Milkwood Arcade), which Apollo's reviewer described as demonstrating her debt to the Monet who found pure joy in colour.
paintings.citation: Michael Fried, 'Morris Louis,' in Art and Objecthood (University of Chicago Press, 1998), 102–121; orig. 1967. Matthew Holman, 'How Monet's water lilies took root across the pond,' Apollo Magazine, July 17, 2018.

paintings.title: Tet
paintings.collection: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
paintings.connection_claim: John Elderfield's 1986 MoMA monograph framed Louis's Veil paintings as the most disciplined inheritance of Monet's submerged greens at the Orangerie: the pigment is no longer applied to the canvas, it has soaked into it, the way Monet's water has no fixed surface. The 2018 Orangerie show paired Louis's Vernal (1960) with Monet's Water Lilies on exactly these grounds, presenting Louis as the painter who took Monet's surface luminosity furthest into pure stain.
paintings.citation: John Elderfield, Morris Louis, exh. cat. (New York: The Museum of Modern Art, 1986); Hearne Pardee, 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet,' The Brooklyn Rail (October 2018).

paintings.title: Towards Disappearance II
paintings.collection: Albright-Knox Art Gallery (now Buffalo AKG), Buffalo, New York
paintings.image_url_comment: Buffalo AKG publishes no open image API. The MoMA catalogue page for the same painting is the authoritative public reference.
paintings.connection_claim: Sam Francis lived in Paris through the 1950s and repeatedly named the Orangerie as the decisive precedent for his mural-scale paintings; Brooklyn Rail's reviewer of the 2018 Orangerie show confirmed he was 'directly inspired by an early experience of Monet's murals.' Critic Peter Selz's 1975 monograph framed Francis's empty white centers ringed by colored patches at the edges as his version of Monet's pond surface, where the colour event happens at the periphery and the middle is held open.
paintings.citation: Peter Selz, Sam Francis (New York: Harry N. Abrams, 1975; rev. ed. 1982); Hearne Pardee, 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet,' The Brooklyn Rail (October 2018).

paintings.title: Dial
paintings.collection: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
paintings.connection_claim: Critic Louis Finkelstein coined the term 'Abstract Impressionism' in a 1956 ARTnews article specifically to describe Guston's pulsing, centre-weighted dabs of pink, red and grey, paint behaving like Monet's late chromatic haze rather than like Pollock's drawn linearity. The 2018 Orangerie show presented Dial as a parallel inheritance to Greenberg's all-over Pollock argument, with Brooklyn Rail's reviewer noting that the canvas 'suggests floating leaves' on a horizonless field.
paintings.citation: Louis Finkelstein, 'New Look: Abstract-Impressionism,' ARTnews 55 (March 1956), 36–39, 66–68; Hearne Pardee, 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet,' The Brooklyn Rail (October 2018).

paintings.title: Painting
paintings.collection: Museum of Modern Art, New York (Philip Johnson Fund, 7.1956)
paintings.connection_claim: Reviewing the 2018 Orangerie show in The Brooklyn Rail, Hearne Pardee observed that although Guston preferred Monet's earlier style, the slow accumulations of marks in Painting evoke the late Water Lilies' liquid surfaces, embodying the existential weight Harold Rosenberg saw concealed under Monet's well-tended pond. Apollo Magazine's Matthew Holman placed the work within curator Cécile Debray's argument that Monet's late, gestural canvases gave postwar American painters a precedent for the canvas as an arena for action.
paintings.citation: Hearne Pardee, 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet,' The Brooklyn Rail (October 2018); Matthew Holman, 'How Monet's water lilies took root across the pond,' Apollo Magazine, July 17, 2018.

paintings.title: Untitled V
paintings.collection: Private collection
paintings.image_url_comment: De Kooning Foundation embargoes most commercial reproductions; no public image API.
paintings.connection_claim: Curators Diane Waldman and Richard Shiff identified de Kooning's late-1970s East Hampton paintings, made on canvases kept wet for weeks, as his attempt to recapture Monet's watery, weather-soaked palette. The 2018 Orangerie show paired his Villa Borghese (1960) with Monet on these grounds; in Untitled V, the long looping pink-yellow-blue strokes are dragged through wet under-paint to produce paint that behaves like weather rather than depicting it.
paintings.citation: Richard Shiff, Between Sense and de Kooning (Reaktion Books, 2011), 142–167; Diane Waldman, Willem de Kooning, exh. cat. (Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, 1988); Hearne Pardee, 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet,' The Brooklyn Rail (October 2018).

paintings.title: Tableau Vert
paintings.collection: Art Institute of Chicago (gift of the artist, 2009)
paintings.image_url_comment: Ellsworth Kelly Foundation controls reproduction; the AIC public collection page hosts a low-res reference image.
paintings.connection_claim: Kelly visited Giverny in August 1952 and was led by Monet's stepson Jean-Pierre Hoschedé into the abandoned Atelier des Nymphéas, where roughly fifteen 20-foot panels stood unseen; he painted Tableau Vert in Paris the next day. The 2014–15 Clark Art Institute exhibition 'Monet | Kelly,' with essays by Yve-Alain Bois and Sarah Lees, framed this as the most direct artist-to-artist transmission of late Monet in twentieth-century painting, and the same painting was hung at the entrance to the 2018 Orangerie show as the most directly Monet-influenced work in the exhibition.
paintings.citation: Yve-Alain Bois and Sarah Lees, Monet | Kelly, exh. cat. (Williamstown, MA: Clark Art Institute / Yale University Press, 2014).

paintings.title: Water Lilies with Japanese Bridge
paintings.medium: screenprinted enamel on processed and swirled stainless steel, with painted aluminum frame
paintings.collection: Roy Lichtenstein Foundation Collection
paintings.image_url_comment: Lichtenstein Foundation strictly licenses all reproductions; the National Galleries of Scotland public page hosts a low-res reference image.
paintings.connection_claim: Lichtenstein's 1992 Water Lilies series reproduces Monet's Japanese Footbridge in Ben-Day dots screenprinted onto stainless steel, an explicit homage that re-reads Monet's pond surface as a reproducible printed sign. In his 1997 interview with David Sylvester, Lichtenstein described wanting 'a way of doing a Monet through just dots that would look like a machine-made impressionist painting'; the polished steel ground also throws the viewer's reflection back into the work, mimicking Monet's pond as a reflective surface.
paintings.citation: Roy Lichtenstein, interview with David Sylvester, in Some Kind of Reality (Anthony d'Offay Gallery, London, 1997); Andrea Theil, 'Water Lilies with Japanese Bridge, 1992,' in Roy Lichtenstein: A Catalogue Raisonné (Roy Lichtenstein Foundation).

paintings.title: Quattro Stagioni: Primavera
paintings.medium: acrylic, oil, crayon and pencil on canvas
paintings.collection: Tate Modern, London
paintings.connection_claim: Curator Jeremy Lewison's 2011–12 traveling exhibition 'Turner Monet Twombly: Later Paintings' presented Twombly's seasonal cycles of dripped crimson, green and ochre as a late-modernist pendant to Monet's year-long pond observations, treating both as cycles of dissolution rather than landscapes. The Quattro Stagioni was hung directly opposite Monet's late water lily studies in the gallery section titled 'The Seasons,' the centerpiece pairing of the show.
paintings.citation: Jeremy Lewison (curator), Turner Monet Twombly: Later Paintings, exh. cat. (Tate Liverpool / Moderna Museet / Staatsgalerie Stuttgart, 2011–12); Richard Leeman, Cy Twombly: A Monograph (Thames & Hudson, 2005), 242–260.

paintings.title: Cold Mountain 6 (Bridge)
paintings.collection: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA)
paintings.connection_claim: Curator Gary Garrels (in MoMA's 2006 retrospective 'Plane Image: A Brice Marden Retrospective') and critic Richard Shiff described Marden's calligraphic, looping Cold Mountain paintings as a late-twentieth-century counterpart to Monet's Japanese Footbridge canvases: an abstraction drawn from arboreal, reflected line rather than from grid or geometry. In Cold Mountain 6 (Bridge), the bridge curve and the reflected willow fronds collapse into a single rhythmic line, the same move Monet made in his 1918–24 paintings of the same site.
paintings.citation: Gary Garrels (ed.), Plane Image: A Brice Marden Retrospective, exh. cat. (New York: Museum of Modern Art, 2006).

paintings.title: Architecture of the Sky III
paintings.collection: Private collection
paintings.connection_claim: Curator Lisa Phillips's 1995 Guggenheim catalogue read Bleckner's dark, dotted, light-pierced fields as late-twentieth-century sky-versions of Monet's cloud-reflection panels at the Orangerie, with the same suspended-light device transposed from water surface to night sky. In Architecture of the Sky III, the dotted points of light on a dark chromatic ground recreate the Orangerie's atmospheric immersion through Symbolist motifs rather than through flat color.
paintings.citation: Lisa Phillips, Ross Bleckner, exh. cat. (New York: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, 1995).

paintings.title: Earthly Paradise
paintings.collection: Art Institute of Chicago
paintings.connection_claim: Bonnard knew Monet personally and lived as his neighbor for the last sixteen years of Monet's life; the two corresponded and exchanged studio visits while Bonnard developed his own approach to dissolving figure into chromatic field. Critic Hearne Pardee, reviewing the 2018 Orangerie show in The Brooklyn Rail, called Bonnard 'Monet's immediate heir,' and the 1948 MoMA Bonnard retrospective (organized by John Rewald) was attended by both Rothko and de Kooning, making Bonnard a recognized French bridge between Monet's color and the American Color Field painters.
paintings.citation: Dore Ashton, About Rothko (Oxford University Press, 1983), 78–80; James Breslin, Mark Rothko: A Biography (University of Chicago Press, 1993), 246; Hearne Pardee, 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet,' The Brooklyn Rail (October 2018).

paintings.title: The Good-bye Door
paintings.collection: Centre Pompidou, Paris (long-term loan to Musée de l'Orangerie at the time of the 2018 exhibition)
paintings.image_url_comment: Centre Pompidou publishes no open IIIF image endpoint. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Hung as the entrance painting to the 2018 Musée de l'Orangerie exhibition 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet,' The Good-bye Door was curator Cécile Debray's opening statement, presenting Mitchell as the polyptych painter most directly continuing Monet's Grandes Décorations format. Apollo Magazine's reviewer Matthew Holman called it the 'knockout work' of the show, and the nine-panel composition was painted from Mitchell's view of the Seine valley at Vétheuil, the same valley Monet had painted from the opposite bank in 1878–81 before moving to Giverny.
paintings.citation: Matthew Holman, 'How Monet's water lilies took root across the pond,' Apollo Magazine, July 17, 2018; Cécile Debray (curator), exh. cat. Nymphéas: L'abstraction américaine et le dernier Monet (Hazan / Musée de l'Orangerie, 2018).

paintings.title: Sunflowers
paintings.collection: Joan Mitchell Foundation / private collection
paintings.image_url_comment: Mitchell Foundation controls reproduction rights; no open API.
paintings.connection_claim: Painted in Mitchell's last years at Vétheuil while she was dying of lung cancer, the Sunflowers diptychs were framed by the 2022 Fondation Louis Vuitton 'Monet–Mitchell' exhibition as her closest engagement with late Monet: blossoms full and chromatic on the left panel, wilting and ghostly on the right, echoing Monet's strategy of painting the same motif under changing conditions. Mitchell had cataract surgery in 1984 and worked through deteriorating peripheral vision in her late polyptychs, just as Monet did in his last decade.
paintings.citation: Suzanne Pagé et al. (eds.), Monet–Mitchell, exh. cat. (Paris: Fondation Louis Vuitton / Hazan, 2022); Sarah Roberts and Katy Siegel (eds.), Joan Mitchell, exh. cat. (San Francisco: SFMOMA / Yale University Press, 2021).

paintings.title: The Arrival of Spring, Normandy, 2020 (No. 340)
paintings.medium: iPad painting, printed on paper at large scale
paintings.dimensions: variable; series of 116 works, hung densely
paintings.collection: Hockney studio / Royal Academy of Arts (2021 exhibition)
paintings.image_url_comment: Rights controlled by David Hockney Inc.
paintings.connection_claim: Hockney moved to a Normandy farmhouse near Monet's Giverny in 2019 and made 116 iPad paintings during the 2020 spring lockdown. In his Royal Academy catalogue text, Hockney himself wrote: 'all the time I was getting better at my mark making on the screen, eventually doing, à la Monet, the water lilies in the pond,' and curator Edith Devaney's 2021 RA exhibition presented the cycle as Hockney's late-style Monet homage, recreating Monet's serial logic of painting one site through changing light.
paintings.citation: David Hockney, exhibition catalogue text for The Arrival of Spring, Normandy, 2020 (Royal Academy of Arts, London, May 23 – September 26, 2021), curated by Edith Devaney.

paintings.title: Homage to Monet 5
paintings.collection: Alex Katz studio / exhibited 2019 Musée de l'Orangerie, Contemporary Counterpoint series
paintings.image_url_comment: Image rights controlled by VAGA / Alex Katz.
paintings.connection_claim: In the Musée de l'Orangerie's 2019 catalogue, Katz himself stated: 'The water lilies are on the pond in Maine and I've been looking at them for 50 years but I never touched them because of Monet. But I said you're going to do it, and I just did it.' Homage to Monet 5 was hung in a single-painting gallery directly adjacent to Monet's panels at the Orangerie as part of the museum's Contemporary Counterpoint series, the most explicit invitation of a contemporary painter into dialogue with Monet's permanent installation.
paintings.citation: Alex Katz, statement and catalogue text for Contemporary Counterpoint 3: Alex Katz. Nymphéas – Homage to Monet, Musée de l'Orangerie, May 15 – September 2, 2019.

paintings.title: Sixteen Waterfalls of Dreams, Memories, and Sentiment
paintings.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
paintings.image_url: /Users/thewildmagnolia/Downloads/moma/Monet experience/src/assets/Sixteen Waterfalls of Dreams, Memories, and Sentiment.jpeg
paintings.image_url_comment: The Met hosts a public image; check current accession URL on metmuseum.org.
paintings.connection_claim: Steir's pour technique, applying thinned oil at the top of a vertical canvas and letting gravity carry the paint downward, produces image and process in one gesture, the way Monet's late water-on-water reflections collapse subject into surface. The 2019 Barnes Foundation exhibition 'Silent Secret Waterfalls,' curated by director Thom Collins, named Monet alongside Cézanne and Van Gogh as Steir's primary historical influences, though Steir herself names John Cage and Chinese ink painting as more direct sources, which is why the connection is curatorial rather than an artist statement.
paintings.citation: Thom Collins (curator), Silent Secret Waterfalls: The Barnes Series, Barnes Foundation, Philadelphia, January 12 – November 17, 2019; Pat Steir interview with Lilly Wei, Studio International (2019).
